Why do we backpropagate?


     •  Let’s think about the problem of w-modific ation, and let’s compare the
        last set of w’s and the first
     •  Last W5: The  output probabilities are directly determined by the Last
        w’s!!!! The  error is very directly determined by the last W’s
     • We can use the error between computed and desired directly to
      determine bette r w’s.
     •  First W2 affe cts its activations, which affe cts another 2 layers of
       activations along with other W’s. It’s really hard to figure out the
       culpability of W2 for the mistakes made all the way at the end!!!!!
      Moreover, the effe ct of W2 on errors INCLUDES the effe ct of W5 on
      them, since W5 is downstream of W2!!!!
     •  So which problem is easier: Improving W2 or W5?
     • W5 is easy! What algorithm do we use to solve small problems then
       bigger ones that depend on them?
     •  Dynamic programming?
     •  Backpropagation is Bellman-Viterbi Dynamic Programming!!!
     •  Backpropagation = SGD + Dynamic programming 😉

The sigmoid activation function

       Lord Edgar Adrian                   σ (z) = 1 / (1 + exp(−z))
    Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, 1932

 Neurons are nearly digital! On or off, roughly.
         If the inner product is large positive,
 sigmoid function is near 1, and if inner product
      Is large negative, sigmois is basically 0.
Animal perception refle cts this: some things that seem
alike, are perceived diffe rent, and some things that are
        Very diffe rent are perceived same!

                 If the inner product is −4:
         σ (−4) = 0.0180

                  If the inner product is 4:
         σ (4) = 0.9820
                                                                                    http s://www.vcalc.com/wiki/vcalc/sigmoid-function

Actual NumPy reference run, seed 0

Requested PyTorch training code
                                                  Final training accuracy: 44.95%import torch  # Tensors
from torch import nn  # Layers and loss
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt  # Plotting
torch.manual_seed(0)  # Initialization                                             100%
X = Formant_Inputs / 1000  # Hz to kHz
y = TrueVowel_Outputs.argmax(1)  # Correct classes
model = nn.Sequential(  # The supplied widths                                                                            80%
    nn.Linear(2, 3, bias=False),  # No bias
    nn.Linear(3, 2, bias=False),  # No bias
    nn.Linear(2, 4, bias=False),  # No bias
                                                                            60%    nn.Linear(4, 5, bias=False),  # Five scores)  # No activations                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      accuracy
loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()  # One-hot cross-entropy
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)  # Plain SGD                        40%
accuracy = []  # Percent correct
for epoch in range(2000):  # Full-batch updates    opt.zero_grad()  # Clear old gradients                                                                                                                                                       Training                                                                            20%
    loss = loss_fn(model(X), TrueVowel_Outputs)  # Forward + loss
    loss.backward()  # Backpropagate
    opt.step()  # Update weights
                                                                       0%    with torch.no_grad():  # Accuracy only                                                                                           0           500         1000         1500         2000
        pred = model(X).argmax(1)  # Largest score wins
        correct = (pred == y).float().mean().item()  # Fraction correct                                 Epoch
        accuracy.append(100 * correct)  # Save percent correct
plt.plot(range(1, 2001), accuracy)  # Accuracy curve
plt.ylim(0, 100)  # Full percent scale
